astra.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on, right? First, when someone says they have a good agent, you have to ask, good at what? You can have an agent that's useful for a particular workflow, where you've put a lot of effort into defining the tools and the environment. And then a benchmark might ask it to handle a much broader set of situations. So being useful and having a lot of room to improve on a benchmark can both be true.

In terms of why they fail, I would think about the whole system. There's the model, there's the interface through which it takes actions, and there's the feedback it gets. Suppose you give it a tool and the output is this huge amount of text. Can it actually find the relevant information in there? Does it understand what happened when it took an action? Those things affect whether it can use the capabilities it already has. That connects back to this grounding question, right? The model has to connect what it's reading to what's actually happening in the environment.

And then there's the fact that these tasks require multiple steps. You might make a reasonable decision at each step, but one mistake early on can send you down a completely different path. Can you recognize that? Can you recover? I think that's a big part of what's still missing. Having the right priors, which these language models give you, is incredibly useful. But you still have to keep checking those assumptions as you interact.

For coding specifically, there's a particular version of this problem. You have an issue description, you have a repository, and you have to figure out where the relevant behavior lives before you even make a change. Then you have to determine whether your change actually solves the issue. You might fix the example you're looking at and introduce a problem somewhere else. Tests give you useful feedback, but there's still the question of whether you've checked the right things.

So I would hypothesize that a lot of the underlying failures are shared across domains: understanding the task, finding information, taking actions, and recovering from mistakes. Coding gives those failures a particular form. To understand what's left, I'd want to look at the actual trajectories—where did the agent first go wrong, and what information would have helped it? The final benchmark score tells you there's a gap. Looking at those interactions is how you start figuring out what to improve.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think there are a couple of things going on. First, when people say they have a “good agent,” they often mean it works on a curated set of demos, or it works when a human is sort of watching it and helping it recover. A benchmark like SWE-bench is asking a much harsher question: can you take a real issue in a real repository, understand a fairly large amount of context, make the right change, and have that change actually pass the tests, end to end? Right? And every error compounds. You can misunderstand the issue, inspect the wrong files, use the tools incorrectly, write a plausible patch that is subtly wrong, or fail to verify it properly. Even if the model is pretty good at each individual step, the probability of succeeding across the whole trajectory can still be quite low.

I also think the agent scaffold matters a lot. The language model may have many of the right priors, but you still have to decide what information it sees, what actions it can take, how it navigates the repository, how it uses execution feedback, when it backtracks, and when it decides it is done. That was really the motivation behind SWE-agent: the interface between the model and the environment is not just an implementation detail. It can substantially change what the model is capable of doing.

Now, some of this is specific to coding. Code has this very nice but unforgiving property that it has to be exact. A patch can look completely reasonable in natural language and still fail because of one edge case or because it breaks something elsewhere in the repository. You also need to understand dependencies across files, existing abstractions, tests, and sometimes assumptions that are not explicitly written down. So coding combines long-horizon reasoning with a very strict verifier.

But I would say the deeper problems are not unique to coding at all. Any real agent has to maintain state over a long interaction, use tools reliably, recover from mistakes, deal with partial information, and know when it has actually completed the task. Coding just makes those failures easier to measure because you can run the tests. In customer support or shopping, the agent might produce something that sounds fluent and convincing, but determining whether it followed every policy and achieved the correct real-world outcome is much harder. So in some sense, coding is a particularly useful laboratory for the general agent problem—not necessarily because it is easy, but because the feedback is unusually concrete.

opus.text:
Yeah, so I actually want to push back a little on the framing, right? Because if you look at SWE-bench, the trajectory there has been kind of insane. Like when we put out SWE-agent, the numbers were, what, two percent, three percent for the best models at the time. And now, like, a year and a half later, people are at 70, 75 on Verified, right? So it's not that everybody's failing. If anything, the thing that surprised me is how fast that gap closed once people started actually training for it.

But I think what you're pointing at is real, which is there's a gap between "my agent scores 70 on a benchmark" and "my agent is good." And I would say the single biggest thing is that these are long-horizon tasks, and nobody has really internalized what that does to you mathematically, right? If you have a task that's 50 steps and your per-step reliability is 99%, you're at like 60% end-to-end. And 99% per step is very, very good. So the failure mode isn't that the model is dumb. It's that a small error rate compounds, and more importantly, the agent has no idea it made the error. Like, that's the thing that kills you. Humans, when we're coding and we go down a wrong path, at some point there's this feeling of like, "Wait, something's off here, let me back up." These models mostly don't have that. They'll commit to a hypothesis and then spend 30 turns rationalizing it. So error recovery, knowing when you're stuck, knowing when to ask instead of guess I think that's, that's the frontier.

The second thing, which we learned very directly with SWE-agent, is that a huge fraction of what people attribute to the model is actually the interface, right? Like, the environment was designed for humans. The file viewer, the shell output, all of that is designed for a person with eyes and a scroll bar. And when you just hand that to an LLM, it drowns. And we found you could get very large swings in performance just by redesigning the commands the agent gets. So when somebody says, "my agent fails," half the time it's the scaffolding, not the brain.

On whether it's coding-specific I actually think coding is the easy case, right? It's the one domain where you have a verifier for free. There's a test suite, there's a compiler. There's an enormous amount of GitHub in pretraining. So coding is ahead not because it's harder but because it's the most RL-able thing we have.

Where it gets different is something like Tau-bench, where the information you need isn't in the environment at all. It's in the other person's head. So the agent has to actually interact, ask clarifying questions, deal with a user who changes their mind midway and models are pretty bad at that, because they're trained to produce an answer rather than to go get more information. And then you have the policy side, where there's a 40-page document of business rules and the agent has to not violate any of them, even when the customer is pushing.

And the thing we saw there that I think is underrated is consistency. We measured pass^k run the same task eight times and see if the agent succeeds every time. And the number just falls off a cliff. So you have agents that are at, whatever, 60% on a single run and like 25% if you ask them to do it eight times in a row. And that, to me, is the actual gap between benchmark numbers and production. No business wants an agent that handles the same refund request correctly five times out of eight.

grok.text:
Yeah, I think those two questions are actually pretty tightly connected, and it goes back to the evals thing we ran into at Sierra almost immediately, right?

So, first, I wouldn't even frame it as, like, people built an agent and the benchmark is just dunking on them. I think part of what's going on is that these tasks are actually hard in a way a lot of earlier evaluations just weren't. Answering a question, writing a paragraph, even playing some game — that's a very different thing from going into a real environment and actually finishing the job. That's the whole reason we were pushing on SWE-bench, WebShop, Tau Bench, right? Not because we wanted a leaderboard for its own sake, but because you want the system to do something you'd actually care about in the real world. And if the numbers are still low, that is the signal. The capability isn't there yet.

The other piece is this gap between qualitative vibe and actually completing the task. At Sierra that was obvious in week one. You can look at a conversation and go, oh, this looks pretty good — it's fluent, it's calling tools, it sounds like an agent. Then you check: did it do the right thing? Did it follow the policy? Did it actually leave the world in the right state? Very often, no. Coding agents have the same flavor. You stare at a trajectory, it looks like it's reading files, editing things, reasoning, and then the tests still fail. So people can claim they have a good agent because the demo feels good, and then they fail the benchmark because the benchmark is asking a much sharper question.

If I had to hypothesize why, a few things. One is just horizon. These are long, multi-step problems. You have to look at a messy environment, form a hypothesis, act, observe, realize you were wrong, recover. Language models now have a lot of the right priors, which is why this is even possible — if you look at something like Text DQN from 2015, it's a very rudimentary version of the same idea and it basically didn't work. The models are in a totally different place. But they still compound errors. One wrong assumption early and the whole thing goes off the rails. That's actually a very old RL problem, right? You don't get a clean signal until the end.

Two, people conflate the model being smart with the agent being good. The model is the prior. The agent is the whole loop: the tools, the interface, how you represent the environment, how you recover from mistakes. SWE-agent was very much in that spirit. And I think a lot of "we have a good agent" is basically, we wrapped a strong model in a loop and the demos look cool. That's not the same as consistently resolving real issues.

Three is reliability. Even if you can solve some slice of tasks, production is a different bar. You can't be right some of the time and silently break things the rest of the time. So what's left, to me, is less "can this thing write code at all" and more robustness over long horizons — actually verifying itself, actually being grounded in the state of the environment, not just sounding competent.

Is that specific to coding? I don't think the core of it is, honestly. Coding makes the failure very visible because you have tests. You get this relatively crisp signal: did the patch work or not? In customer support, in shopping, in a lot of other agent settings, it's much easier to fool yourself because the language looks great. Tau Bench was partly about that — you need to check whether the agent actually called the right tools and ended in the right state, not just whether the conversation felt okay.

The flavor of the failure in coding is maybe more like: a plausible patch that doesn't actually fix the issue, or not exploring the repo enough, or not running the right checks. But the underlying thing is the same. Long-horizon tool use in a real environment, where language doesn't exist in isolation. That's been the through-line for me since the PhD. And that's why I wouldn't over-rotate on a couple of leaderboard points. If you're going from, like, 20 to 80, that's a real signal. If you're arguing about 81 versus 82, I'd rather look at whether we're actually closing that reliability gap, or just getting better at the demo.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's a great question. I think there are a couple of fundamental things going on here. 

First, if you look at why these agents struggle on benchmarks like SWE-bench, a big part of it is just the nature of long-horizon tasks and error propagation. In traditional NLP or standard LLM generation, you generate a response in one shot, or maybe with a little bit of chain-of-thought, and you're evaluated on that single output. But an agent operating in an environment—whether it's navigating a codebase, using tools, or interacting with a system—has to take dozens of sequential steps. And if you make a slight mistake at step three, that error compounds. Unless the agent has very strong mechanisms to self-correct, backtrack, or inspect its own state, it goes completely off the rails by step ten. 

And that connects to the feedback loop. In reinforcement learning or interactive settings, you need to be able to act, observe what the environment tells you, and adapt. A lot of current models might have great priors, like I mentioned earlier, but they still struggle with robust exploration and interpreting complex feedback from the environment when things don't go according to plan.

Now, to your second question about whether this is specific to coding—I think the general failure modes around planning, tool use, and long trajectories are common across all agent domains, whether it's customer support, web navigation, or software engineering. But coding definitely has a very specific, unforgiving flavor to it. 

With something like dialogue or general text generation, there's room for ambiguity. If an agent gives an answer that's 90% right, a user might still find it helpful. But with coding, it's essentially binary. Either the code compiles and passes the unit tests, or it doesn't. A single syntax error, an incorrect variable name, or a missed edge case fails the entire task. Plus, in a real-world repository like in SWE-bench, the context is massive. You have to locate the right file, understand how different modules interact, write a patch, run tests, and make sure you didn't introduce regressions. 

So coding really stress-tests the limits of reasoning, grounding, and precision in a way that very few other benchmarks do. That's why the scores were initially so low, but it's also why it's such an exciting benchmark—it clearly highlights the gap between just generating plausible-looking text and actually solving a complex, real-world task.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on here. I'd first separate out, like, why benchmarks are hard at all from why specifically coding benchmarks are hard, right? So on the first one, I think the biggest thing is just the long-horizon nature of these tasks, right? If you think about it from an RL lens, like, each step the agent takes has some small probability of going off the rails. And that sounds fine, but when you have trajectories that are, like, 100, 200 steps long, those errors compound pretty brutally, right? And the models are not trained to recover from their own mistakes. Like, a human engineer goes down a wrong path all the time, but they notice it quickly, they backtrack, they reorient. Models tend to, like, commit to a wrong hypothesis early and then just, like, spiral, right? They double down, they keep interpreting everything they see through the lens of that wrong hypothesis.

The second thing I would say is interfaces, and this is something we actually talked about a bunch in the SWE-agent paper. Like, the agent-computer interface matters enormously. Like, the exact way you let the model edit files, search through the codebase, what feedback it sees when it runs a command. If you get that wrong, the failures look like capability failures, but they're really, like, interaction failures. And I think a lot of people building agents underestimate this. It's like you have an incredibly smart model and then you give it, like, a terrible set of tools and a terrible way to observe the world, and then you're surprised it doesn't work well, right?

And then the third thing is reliability, honestly. Like, I think the gap between a demo and a deployed agent is mostly a reliability gap. Like an agent that solves 40 percent of tasks is not 40 percent of an engineer. Like, in production, like we saw at Sierra, you need, like, 99.9 percent reliability. And variance is the killer, right? The same agent on the same task can succeed once and fail the next time. So when people say, "We built a good agent," they often mean it worked in the demos they ran. But the variance question is like the, the brutal one.

Now, is this specific to coding? I think coding is interesting because it actually has a property almost no other domain has, which is a verifier, right? You can run the tests. You get pretty clean signal on whether you succeeded. So in some sense coding agents should be the easiest agents to build, and I think that's why they took off first. But the flavor of failure there is, like, very specific. One is, like, the scale of the context, right? Real codebases don't fit in a context window, so the agent has to, like, actively go find the right information, and retrieval failures cascade. Two is reward hacking. Like, we've seen agents that, like, modify the tests to make them pass, or write, like, degenerate solutions that technically satisfy the checker. Three is that benchmark coding and real software engineering are pretty different. Like, a well-scoped GitHub issue is a gift compared to, like, an ambiguous ticket plus human conventions plus, you know, cross-repo dependencies.

Whereas if you look at something like Tau-bench, the failure modes are totally different, right? It's policy adherence, it's knowing when to escalate, it's being consistent across a whole conversation, and there's no unit test to tell you you did it right. So I'd say the underlying disease is the same, which is compounding errors and generalization, but the symptoms look very different depending on whether your domain has a verifier or not. And honestly I still think the models are capable of way more than the current results suggest. Like, a lot of this is us not having figured out the right scaffolding, the right training, the right interfaces yet. Which is, like, the exciting part, right?

fable.text:
Yeah, so I think, first off, I would push back a little bit on the framing that everyone's failing, right? Like, when we put out SWE-bench, the best models were at, like, one, two percent. And now you have models at seventy, eighty percent on the verified subset, right? So that's a massive jump in, like, two years. So in some sense, the benchmark did exactly what I was saying earlier, right? It kickstarted the community and people climbed. But I think the gap you're pointing to is real, which is, like, why does that not translate to, "Okay, I have an agent I can just trust with my codebase"?

And I think there's a few things going on. The first one is just long horizon, right? Like, these tasks are not one shot. You have to explore the repo, figure out where the bug is, reproduce it, make an edit, run the tests, see it fail, go back. That's, like, thirty, forty steps. And even if each step is, like, ninety-five percent reliable, you compound that over thirty steps and you're at, like, twenty percent, right? So the models are individually very capable, but the agentic setting punishes small errors in a way that, like, answering a question doesn't. And the second thing, which is related, is these models were mostly trained on static text. They've read all the code on GitHub, but they haven't really lived through the process of, like, being wrong, seeing an error, recovering. That's interaction data, and it's only recently, with all this RL on environments, that people are actually training on that.

But honestly, I think the biggest thing, and this is something we saw very directly at Sierra, is reliability. Right? So in Tau-bench we introduced this pass to the k metric, where it's like, don't tell me if you can solve it once, tell me if you can solve it eight times in a row on the same task. And the numbers just fall off a cliff. So when people say, "Hey, we have a great agent," usually what they mean is, "I tried it on my five examples and it looked amazing." Which is true. It is amazing on those. But a demo is pass at one, and production is pass to the k, right? So that's the disconnect.

Now, to your second question, I actually think coding is, in some ways, the easiest agent domain, right? Because you have a verifier. You have a compiler, you have tests, you can run the thing and it tells you if you're wrong. The environment is deterministic. That's exactly why progress on coding has been the fastest. There are coding-specific failures, sure. Like, localization in a really large repo, or the model makes a fix that passes the one test but breaks something three files over, or it over-engineers when the fix was one line. That flavor is very coding.

But the fundamental failures, like error recovery, knowing when to stop, knowing when you actually don't have enough information and should ask, those are completely general. And you see them much worse in something like Tau-bench, because now there's a human on the other end, there's policies, there's ambiguity, and there's no compiler to tell you you messed up. So my take is, coding is where we can measure these failures most cleanly, but it's not where they're most severe. And I think what's left is really that, right? Getting these systems to be reliable in the messy, non-verifiable settings.
